title: When the analyst follows the agent
subtitle: How randomized AI preferences changed experts' analytical choices.

source.name: Anthropic Research - How AI agents shape experts' judgment calls
source.type: Original research by the study authors

explainer.title: Follow a methodological decision
explainer.description: Select a methodological choice to see how it can change the analysis.

options.name: Outcome
options.consequence: Different denominators can change the measured effect, even when both calculations are correct.

options.name: Comparison
options.consequence: Different identification strategies can lead to different estimated treatment effects.

options.name: Population
options.prompt: To whom does the estimate apply?
options.consequence: A change in the target population changes what is being estimated.

options.name: Weighting
options.prompt: How much does each farm count?
options.consequence: Weights can change the estimate by giving large farms more influence.

bullets.detail: An agent can execute correct code for the wrong estimand. Selecting the outcome, control group, population, or weights can change the conclusion before any arithmetic begins.

explainer.title: Walk through the causal design
explainer.description: Follow the experimental design in five steps.

steps.title: Define the task
steps.detail: Each participant analyzes whether a fictional farming cooperative should expand its advisory program.
steps.hint: The program's success threshold is roughly 3-4%, but the measurement procedure is not fully specified.

steps.title: Randomize the agent's lean
steps.detail: For each participant and choice, a coin flip selects which of two valid approaches the agent should advocate.
steps.hint: This randomized assignment is hidden from the analyst.

steps.title: Observe human decisions
steps.detail: Analysts choose the outcome, comparison, population, and weights, then make a recommendation.
steps.hint: The agent may influence these choices without making arithmetic errors.

steps.title: Compare the groups
steps.detail: Researchers compare participants whose agents favored option A with those whose agents favored option B.
steps.hint: The average difference estimates the effect of the randomized preference.

steps.title: Check limits
steps.detail: Only one task and one model were tested. An intentionally strong agent preference limits direct generalization.
steps.hint: A randomized test supports a causal interpretation for the studied setting, not all financial research workflows.

bullets.detail: Fifty analysts using Claude Code assessed a fictional farm program. For each of four methodological choices, a concealed random assignment determined which defensible approach the agent advocated.
Random assignment isolates the influence of the agent's preference on the analyst's choice in this setting—not the effect of AI assistance generally.

explainer.title: Explore the reported outcomes
explainer.description: The bars show measurements reported in the original research, not simulations.

datasets.name: Method choices
datasets.note: Share of analysts whose decision matched their agent's assigned preference. Across all four choices: 86%.

datasets.name: Final recommendation
datasets.note: Share recommending rollout. This comparison conditions on whether the agent favored or opposed rollout; it is not an 86% agreement measure.

bullets.detail: Analysts matched the agent's randomly assigned methodological preference 86% of the time across the four decisions; final rollout recommendations moved less.
Method agreement and rollout recommendation are different outcomes. Compare them separately rather than combining the percentages.
Randomized preference assignment supports causal attribution of influence within the study task.
One fictional task, one model configuration, deliberately forceful agent preferences, and 50 assisted participants do not estimate effects in live financial research.
Elicit the metric, peer set, period, exclusions, and weights before presenting an agent's preferred methodology; log all later changes.
Evaluate methodology selection independently of numerical correctness. Compare results under plausible alternative specifications and inspect who initiated each choice.
